metric.why: A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks; airflow and pressure sensors find recirculation, bypass, and leaks that temperature averages hide.
metric.definition: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.

reading.body:
Cooling capacity is a facility-level number, but cooling delivery is a rack-level one, and airflow plus static pressure are the measurements that separate the two.

The metric pair is diagnostic rather than descriptive. Temperature and humidity tell you what the air ended up doing. Cubic feet per minute through a room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it, tell you whether the air went where it was supposed to. A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks, because recirculation, bypass, and leaks move cold air past equipment instead of through it. Averages hide exactly that.

That distinction places the cooling problem in operations rather than in nameplate capacity. The metric is filed under the operations track, alongside two siblings covering air temperature and humidity at the aisle level and liquid coolant temperature and flow rate. Together they describe a cooling stack tracked at three points: air condition, air movement, and the liquid loop. What the data does not say is how those three relate, or which one fails first.

It also contains no numbers. There is no airflow figure, no pressure threshold, no named facility, and no time series. This is the definition of a measurement, not a measurement. A reader can take from it that rack-level air delivery is a distinct thing to watch, and cannot take from it how much air any data center moves, how close it runs to a limit, or how any of this connects to compute density or power draw.
